keyPoints: Use the determinant formula for the cross product.
Interchanging the two vectors reverses the sign of the cross product.
modelAnswer: (i) a×b=4i−15j−7k and b×a=−4i+15j+7k=−(a×b). (ii) a×b=30i+11j−27k and b×a=−30i−11j+27k=−(a×b). (iii) a×b=4i−6j+2k and b×a=−4i+6j−2k=−(a×b). Thus the cross product is anti-commutative in every case.

modelAnswer: (i) a×b=−18i−8j+3k. Its dot products are (a×b)·a=−54+48+6=0 and (a×b)·b=−36+24+12=0, so it is perpendicular to both. (ii) a×b=3i+15j+6k. Its dot products are (a×b)·a=12−30+18=0 and (a×b)·b=3+15−18=0, so it is perpendicular to both.

Resolve a vector using projection onto the given direction.
modelAnswer: (i) a×b=8i+37j+10k, so a vector of magnitude 5 perpendicular to both is ±(5/√1533)(8i+37j+10k). (ii) For v=5i+2j−3k and u=2i−j+3k, v·u=−1 and |u|²=14. The parallel component is (v·u/|u|²)u=−u/14=−i/7+j/14−3k/14; the perpendicular component is v−parallel=36i/7+27j/14−39k/14.

keyPoints: Magnitude=sqrt(38)
Unit vector=(i-j+6k)/sqrt(38)
Diagonal lengths=sqrt(5), 3
modelAnswer: Let a=(1,-2,1), b=(1,-1,-1), and c=(2,0,1). Then 2a-3b+c=(1,-1,6), whose magnitude is sqrt(38). The required unit vector is (i-j+6k)/sqrt(38). The parallelogram diagonals are (i+j)+(i-2j)=2i-j and (i+j)-(i-2j)=3j, so their lengths are sqrt(5) and 3.
stem:
(i) If $\vec{a}=\hat{\imath}-2 \hat{\jmath}+\widehat{k} ; \vec{b}=\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2 \hat{\imath}+\hat{k}$ then find a unit vector in the direction of $2 \vec{a}-3 \vec{b}+\vec{c}$.
    (ii) Use vectors to find the length of diagonals of a parallelogram having adjacent sides $\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}$ and $\hat{\imath}-2 \hat{\jmath}$.

keyPoints: Lagrange’s identity follows by expanding the cross-product components.
A vector perpendicular to both inputs is a scalar multiple of their cross product.
modelAnswer: (i) If a=(a₁,a₂,a₃) and b=(b₁,b₂,b₃), expand |a×b|² as the sum of squares of the three 2×2 minors. Collecting terms gives (a₁²+a₂²+a₃²)(b₁²+b₂²+b₃²)−(a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃)²=|a|²|b|²−(a·b)². (ii) A vector perpendicular to both a and b is d=t(a×b). Here a×b=−2i−j+4k and c·(a×b)=5, so t=1/5. Thus d=−(2/5)i−(1/5)j+(4/5)k.
stem:
(i) Show that the points with position vectors $\hat{i}-\hat{j}, 4 \hat{i}-3 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $2 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}+5 \hat{k}$ are the vertices of a right-angled triangle.
    (ii) Show that the triangle with $2 \hat{\imath}+3 \hat{\jmath}+\sqrt{3} \hat{k}, \sqrt{10} \hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}+\sqrt{5} \hat{k}$ and $-3 \hat{\imath}+\sqrt{3} \hat{\jmath}+2 \hat{k}$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle.

keyPoints: A cross product is perpendicular to each input vector.
Two nonzero vectors are parallel exactly when their cross product is zero.
modelAnswer: (i) No such vector b exists as written: every a×b must be perpendicular to a, but a·c=(1)(1)+(−2)(1)+(3)(−1)=−4≠0. Thus a×b cannot equal c. (ii) Compute (a−d)×(b−c)=a×b−a×c−d×b+d×c. Since a×c=b×d, the middle terms cancel; since a×b=c×d=−d×c, the remaining terms cancel. Hence (a−d)×(b−c)=0. With the stated nonzero differences, a−d is parallel to b−c.
stem:
(i) Find the value of $\lambda$ for which $|\vec{a}|=|3 \vec{b}|$ where $\vec{a}=\hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}+\lambda \widehat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{b}}=\hat{\imath}+2 \hat{\jmath}-\hat{k}$.
    (ii) If $\vec{a}=2 \hat{\imath}+3 \hat{\jmath}$ and $\vec{b}=-3 \hat{\imath}+2 \hat{\jmath}$. Check whether $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|$ or $\vec{a}=\vec{b}$.

keyPoints: A vector both parallel and perpendicular to a nonzero vector must be zero.
Use c=−a−b and anti-commutativity of the cross product.
modelAnswer: (i) Put u=b−c. The two hypotheses give a·u=0 and a×u=0. Since a is nonzero, a×u=0 makes u parallel to a, while a·u=0 makes u perpendicular to a; hence u=0 and b=c. (ii) From a+b+c=0, c=−a−b. Then b×c=b×(−a−b)=−b×a=a×b, and c×a=(−a−b)×a=−b×a=a×b. Therefore a×b=b×c=c×a.
stem:
If $\vec{a}=2 \hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}+5 \hat{k}$ then find:
    (i) A vector of magnitude 5 in the direction $\vec{a}-2 \vec{b}$.

keyPoints: The magnitude of a cross product of unit vectors is the sine of their included angle.
Use Lagrange’s identity to recognize the Gram determinant.
modelAnswer: (i) Since b and c are unit vectors with angle π/6, |b×c|=sin(π/6)=1/2. The vector b×c is perpendicular to both b and c, as is the unit vector a. Hence a is parallel or antiparallel to b×c, and a=±(b×c)/|b×c|=±2(b×c). (ii) By Lagrange’s identity, |a×b|²=|a|²|b|²−(a·b)², which is exactly the displayed 2×2 determinant.
stem:
The position vectors of points A and B are $\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$ respectively.
    (i) Find the position vector of point P dividing the line segment joining A and B in the ratio 2 : 3 internally.
    (ii) Find the position vector of point Q dividing the line segment $\overline{A B}$ in the ratio 3 : 2 externally.

keyPoints: Apply Lagrange’s identity.
Taking a square root of (a·b)² leaves a possible plus or minus sign.
modelAnswer: Use |a×b|²=|a|²|b|²−(a·b)². (i) |a×b|²=3²·5²−(15/4)²=3375/16, so |a×b|=15√15/4. (ii) (a·b)²=2²·5²−8²=36, so a·b=±6. The given magnitudes alone do not determine its sign.
stem:
(i) The three vertices of a parallelogram ABCD taken in order are $A(3,-4)$; $B(-1,-3)$ and $C(-6,2)$. Find the fourth vertex $D$.
    (ii) Find the values of $x$ and $y$ if $A(1,2) ; B(4, y) ; C(x, 6)$ and $D(3,5)$ taken in order are the vertices of a parallelogram.

keyPoints: Parallelogram area is the magnitude of a cross product.
Triangle area is half the magnitude of the cross product of two side vectors.
modelAnswer: (i) a×b=−19i−13j−k, so the parallelogram area is |a×b|=√531=3√59. (ii) With P=(1,−1,1), Q=(2,1,2), R=(3,0,−1), PQ=(1,2,1) and PR=(2,1,−2). Their cross product is (−5,6,−3), so triangle area is √70/2. The side lengths are |PQ|=√6, |PR|=3, |QR|=√11. Thus ∠P=cos⁻¹(2/(3√6)), ∠Q=cos⁻¹(4/√66), and ∠R=cos⁻¹(7/(3√11)).
stem: Show that the line segments joining the mid points of the sides of a quadrilateral consecutively form a parallelogram.

keyPoints: A parallelogram’s area is half the magnitude of the cross product of its diagonals.
Translate the triangle to the origin and expand the cross product.
modelAnswer: (i) For diagonals p=3i+j−2k and q=i−3j+4k, adjacent sides are (p+q)/2 and (p−q)/2, so the parallelogram area is |p×q|/2. Since p×q=−2i−14j−10k, the area is √300/2=5√3. (ii) Using AB=b−a and AC=c−a, triangle area is 1/2|(b−a)×(c−a)|=1/2|a×b+b×c+c×a|.
stem: Show that line segments joining the mid points of the diagonals and the mid points of any two opposite sides of a quadrilateral consecutively form a parallelogram.

keyPoints: A zero cross product means the vectors are parallel or one is zero.
A zero dot product means nonzero vectors are perpendicular; parallel and perpendicular nonzero vectors are impossible.
modelAnswer: Since a×b=0, a and b are parallel (or one is zero). If both were nonzero, parallel vectors could not also have a·b=0. Therefore at least one of a and b is the zero vector; equivalently, a=0 or b=0 (including the case both are zero).
stem: Prove that line segments joining the midpoint of the diagonals of a trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides and its length is half the difference of the lengths of the parallel sides.

keyPoints: PS=s-r
OQ=r+s
A non-zero scalar multiple proves parallelism
modelAnswer: Using the three equilateral triangles, OP is parallel and equal to SQ, so OQ=OS+SQ=s+r. Also PS=OS-OP=s-r, and QR is parallel and equal to PS. Since M is the midpoint of QR, QM=1/2(s-r), so SM=SQ+QM=r+1/2(s-r)=1/2(r+s)=1/2 OQ. Thus SM is a scalar multiple of OQ, so OQ is parallel to SM.

Solve the cross-product component equations for the unknown application point.
modelAnswer: Let r=(2,1,−3)−(−1,−1,1)=(3,2,−4). The stated moment direction d=(6,−21,−6) has |d|=3√57 and r·d=0, so the moment vector is M=d/3=(2,−7,−2). The minimum force is perpendicular to r: F=(M×r)/|r|²=(32,2,25)/29 N, with magnitude |F|=√(57/29) N. (ii) Let r=(x,y,z) be measured from (−1,2,−3). Solving r×(2,2,−3)=(3,−2,1) gives r=(−17/10,−7/5,3/5), so the application point is (−27/10,3/5,−12/5).

If $\vec{a}=2 \hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}+\hat{k} ; \vec{b}=\hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}+4 \hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=-\hat{\imath}-2 \hat{\jmath}+5 \hat{k}$, then evaluate the followings.

Compute each cross product separately, then add the moments.
modelAnswer: The displacement vectors from the fixed point are r₁=(4,3,0) and r₂=(−4,−3,−6). Therefore M₁=r₁×F₁=(15,−20,7), M₂=r₂×F₂=(−9,−26,19), and the net moment is M₁+M₂=(6,−46,26).

keyPoints: Write each scalar triple product as the determinant with the three vectors as columns.
Cyclic column permutations preserve a determinant.
Hence all three scalar triple products are equal.
modelAnswer: The scalar triple product is the determinant [a b c]. A cyclic permutation of the three columns is an even permutation, so det[a b c]=det[b c a]=det[c a b]. Therefore a·(b×c)=b·(c×a)=c·(a×b).
stem:
(i) If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are three vectors such that $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=0$ and $|\vec{a}|=2 ;|\vec{b}|=3$ and $|\vec{c}|=4$ then find angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.
    (ii) If $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|=|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|$, then find angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

keyPoints: Represent the scalar triple product as a determinant.
An odd transposition reverses determinant sign.
Apply this to the two displayed reversals.
modelAnswer: Let T=a·(b×c)=det[a b c]. Swapping two columns changes the determinant sign, so det[b a c]=-T and det[a c b]=-T. Therefore a·(b×c)=-b·(a×c)=-a·(c×b).

(i) If $\vec{a}=\hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}+4 \hat{k} ; \vec{b}=7 \hat{\imath}-9 \hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=3 \hat{\imath}-2 \hat{\jmath}+5 \hat{k}$, find the value of $\lambda$ so that $\vec{a}-\lambda \vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{c}$.
    (ii) Show that the angle between any two diagonals of a cube is $\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)$.

keyPoints: Three vectors are coplanar iff their scalar triple product is zero.
The first determinant evaluates to zero.
The second determinant is 15−2λ, giving λ=15/2.
modelAnswer: Use the scalar triple product. For (i), b×c=(-18,-6,2), so a·(b×c)=72+36−108=0; hence the vectors are coplanar. For (ii), a·(b×c)=15−2λ, so coplanarity gives λ=15/2.
stem:

Also find their vector projections.

keyPoints: Use a scalar triple product for point coplanarity.
The point parameter is λ=2.
Set the determinant of the three structured vectors to zero and divide by the nonzero factors.
modelAnswer: For the four points to be coplanar, [(B−A),(C−A),(D−A)]=0. Here B−A=(4,λ−4,−2), C−A=(−2,4,−2), D−A=(−2,−2,4), and (C−A)×(D−A)=(12,12,12). Thus the triple product is 12λ−24, so λ=2. For (ii), expand the determinant of (a,b,c): (1−α)(1−β)(1−γ)−(1−α)−(1−β)−(1−γ)+2? Direct simplification of the zero determinant gives (1−β)(1−γ)+(1−α)(1−γ)+(1−α)(1−β)=(1−α)(1−β)(1−γ), and division by the nonzero product yields the stated reciprocal identity.
stem:
(i) Three vertices of triangle are $A(0,-1,-2) ; B(3,1,4)$ and $C(5,7,1)$. Show that ABC is a right-angled triangle and find the other two angles.
    (ii) A vector $\vec{r}$ is equally inclined with the coordinate axes and $|\vec{r}|=5$. Find the vector $\vec{r}$.

keyPoints: Coplanarity is preserved by the displayed linear column transformation.
The scalar triple product magnitude is the parallelogram area times the perpendicular unit component.
sin(π/6)=1/2 gives the stated square.
modelAnswer: If c=αa+βb, then the columns a+b, b+c, c+a are obtained from columns a,b,c by a linear column transformation with determinant 2. Hence their scalar triple product is 2[a b c]=0, so they are coplanar. Also, because c is perpendicular to a and b and is a unit vector, [a b c]=c·(a×b) has magnitude |a||b|sin(π/6)=|a||b|/2. Squaring gives [a b c]^2=|a|^2|b|^2/4.
stem:
(i) If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are three vectors such that $|\vec{a}|=2 ;|\vec{b}|=5 ;|\vec{c}|=4$ and $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=0$ then find the value of $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}$
    (ii) For any vector $\vec{r}$ prove that $\vec{r}=(\vec{r} . \hat{\imath}) \hat{\imath}+(\vec{r} . \hat{\jmath}) \hat{\jmath}+(\vec{r} . \hat{k}) \hat{k}$

The first determinant is zero.
The second determinant has magnitude 68.
modelAnswer: The parallelepiped volume is the absolute scalar triple product. For set (i), b×c=(5,−10,−5), so a·(b×c)=0 and V=0. For set (ii), b×c=(6,−9,4), so a·(b×c)=−68 and V=68 cubic units.
stem: The dot products of $\vec{r}$ with the vectors $\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3 \hat{k} ; \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}-2 \hat{k}$ and $2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+4 \hat{k}$ are 0,5 and 8 respectively. Find the vector $\vec{r}$.

keyPoints: Expand both squared magnitudes
Subtract to obtain the dot-product identity
Add to obtain the parallelogram law
modelAnswer: Expand the squared magnitudes using the dot product: |a+b|^2=|a|^2+2(a·b)+|b|^2 and |a-b|^2=|a|^2-2(a·b)+|b|^2. Subtracting gives |a+b|^2-|a-b|^2=4(a·b), hence a·b=1/4|a+b|^2-1/4|a-b|^2. Adding the two expansions gives |a+b|^2+|a-b|^2=2|a|^2+2|b|^2, hence |a|^2+|b|^2=1/2|a+b|^2+1/2|a-b|^2.

(i) Let the unit vectors be u and v. Since |u+v|=1, 1=|u+v|²=2+2u·v, so u·v=−1/2. Therefore |u−v|²=2−2u·v=3 and |u−v|=√3. (ii) An angle in a semicircle subtends a diameter; by the inscribed-angle theorem it is 90°.
stem:

keyPoints: Parallel component ratios give λ=2/3.
The dot product condition gives λ=−3/20 for perpendicularity.
modelAnswer: For parallel vectors, compare components: 3/1=(-2)/(−λ)=6/(3λ), giving λ=2/3. For perpendicular vectors, a·b=3+2λ+18λ=3+20λ=0, giving λ=−3/20.
stem:

    (ii) Prove that angle bisectors of triangle are concurrent.

keyPoints: Form the sum and difference vectors.
Use the dot-product projection formula.
Scalar component is √2; vector projection is (−1,1,0).
modelAnswer: a+b=(−2,0,8) and a−b=(−4,4,0). The scalar component along a−b is ((a+b)·(a−b))/|a−b|=8/(4√2)=√2. The corresponding vector projection is ((a+b)·(a−b))/|a−b|²(a−b)=(−1,1,0).

keyPoints: Use the difference of squares identity for dot products.
The unit-vector condition gives |v|²=1.
Therefore |u|=√19.
modelAnswer: Expand the dot product: (u−v)·(u+v)=|u|²−|v|². Since v is a unit vector, |v|²=1, so |u|²−1=18 and |u|=√19.
stem:
(i) The resultant of two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$ and $|\vec{a}|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}|\vec{b}|$. Show that resultant of $7 \vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$.
    (ii) Prove that $\hat{a}+\hat{b}$ is equally inclined with $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

keyPoints: Form the sum vector and its norm.
Use the unit vector w/|w|.
The sign check selects λ=2/9.
modelAnswer: The summed vector is w=(λ+2,−5,4). The scalar product with (1,1,−1) is (λ−7)/|w|, so set (λ−7)/√((λ+2)^2+41)=−1. Squaring gives (λ−7)^2=(λ+2)^2+41, hence λ=2/9; it satisfies the required negative sign.
stem: A force of $\vec{F}=3 \hat{\imath}-5 \hat{\jmath}+7 \hat{k}$ newtons is applied on a body and moves it at a distance of 14 meters in the direction of the vector $\hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}$. How much work is done?

keyPoints: Write a in components.
Evaluate the three cross-product magnitudes.
Their sum is twice the squared norm.
modelAnswer: Let a=(x,y,z). Then |a×i|²=y²+z², |a×j|²=x²+z², and |a×k|²=x²+y². Adding gives 2(x²+y²+z²)=2|a|².

keyPoints: Express triangle area using a cross product.
Use the corresponding included angle at each vertex.
All three ratios equal abc/(2Δ).
modelAnswer: Let side vectors be u=AB and v=AC, with included angle α. The area is Δ=1/2|u×v|=1/2bc sin α, so a/sin α=bc/ (2Δ). Applying the same area formula at the other vertices gives b/sin β=c/sin γ=abc/(2Δ), proving the sine rule.
